In product reviews, ask engineering how prompts are structured: is there a system prompt with clear rules, are user inputs separated from instructions (which also helps against prompt injection), is output validated against a schema? These questions signal real technical understanding.

p: A hallucination is an output that sounds right but is false or unsupported: a made-up statistic, a non-existent policy clause, a fake citation. It happens because a model generates the most plausible continuation, not a verified fact. When it lacks the information, a plausible-sounding answer is still the most likely text.

steps: Explicitly permit and encourage the model to say when information isn't available. This alone reduces false answers a lot.
Provide the documents and instruct: answer only from these.
For long documents, ask the model to extract exact quotes first, then answer from the quotes.
Each claim must point to a source; claims without one are removed.
Run the same prompt several times (inconsistency signals hallucination), or have a second step check claims against sources.
For high-stakes outputs (legal, medical, financial), a person approves before use.

p: Without controls, a customer asks about refunds for damaged goods and the bot invents a 60-day window. The real policy is 30 days. That's a promise the company may have to honour.

With controls: the bot retrieves the refund policy, answers only from it, cites section 3.2, and if the question isn't covered says 'I can't find that in our policy; let me connect you to an agent'. A weekly sample of conversations is reviewed for accuracy.

bullets: Never promise 'zero hallucinations'; promise measured rates and controls.
Define the fallback behaviour when the answer isn't known.
Track groundedness and user-reported errors as product metrics.

p: Hallucination risk is the top concern in AI steering committees. Bring a structured answer: risk level by use case, controls in place (grounding, citations, refusal when unknown, human review), how you measure (sampled audits, automated groundedness scoring, user feedback) and the escalation path when errors are found.

Design the 'I don't know' experience deliberately. A good fallback (hand off to a human, link to the source, ask a clarifying question) keeps trust high. A bot that always answers confidently loses trust after the first visible mistake.

mis: Newer models don't hallucinate.
They hallucinate less but still do.
Hallucinations are random bugs that can be fully fixed.
They're inherent to how models generate text; you manage the rate.
Citations prove correctness.
Citations can be wrong or misread; check them.

Comparing several runs to detect inconsistency.
What happens when the AI can't answer.

Inconsistent answers flag likely hallucinations.

p: Grounding means making the model answer from specific trusted sources (your documents, a database, live search results) instead of from its general training memory. It turns a closed-book exam into an open-book one, and ideally the student also shows which page they used.

table: Your files via RAG or upload

p: NotebookLM only answers from the sources you upload and shows numbered citations you can click to see the exact passage. Upload three project documents and ask ten questions; check each citation. You'll notice it says when something isn't in the sources, and that answer quality depends on what you uploaded. That's grounding in action.

Faithfulness or groundedness is the share of claims in an answer that are supported by the provided sources. Evaluation tools can score it automatically by checking each claim against the retrieved text. It's distinct from correctness: an answer can be faithful to an outdated document and still be wrong, which is why source quality matters.

bullets: Make 'answers must cite approved sources' a requirement for enterprise assistants.
Assign owners for source documents; grounding is only as good as the sources.
Track groundedness alongside user satisfaction.

p: For enterprise assistants, grounding is also a governance question: which sources are approved, who owns each, how often are they reviewed, and how are outdated documents removed? A content governance plan is often the missing piece in AI assistant projects.
When demoing grounded assistants to stakeholders, show the citations and click through them. It builds trust faster than any accuracy statistic, and shows exactly where quality depends on content.

Uploading documents means the model learned them.
It reads them in context; nothing is permanently learned.
Search grounding is always current.
It depends on what the search returns and how it's filtered.

Link from a claim to its source.

What does faithfulness measure?
How much of the answer is supported by the given sources.
Example of tool grounding?

p: An embedding turns a piece of text into a list of numbers (a vector), often hundreds or thousands long, so that texts with similar meaning have similar numbers. 'Cheap flights to Goa' and 'low-cost airfare to Goa' share few words but land close together. 'Python programming' and 'python snake' land far apart despite sharing a word.

steps: Run each document chunk through an embedding model; store the vectors.
Turn the user's question into a vector with the same model.
Measure closeness, usually cosine similarity. Closest vectors = most similar meaning.
The best matches feed search results, RAG, recommendations or duplicate detection.

p: Imagine a map with only two dimensions: one for 'royalty' and one for 'fruitiness'. King and queen sit together high on royalty; apple and banana sit together high on fruitiness. Real embeddings have hundreds of dimensions capturing many aspects of meaning at once, which can't be named so neatly, but the principle is the same: nearness means similarity.

p: Embedding choices are rarely discussed by stakeholders but have long-term consequences. In design reviews ask: which embedding model, tested on what queries, in which languages, and what's the plan if we switch? Re-embedding a large corpus costs time and money and needs a migration plan.

Embeddings power more than RAG: duplicate ticket detection, similar-case recommendations, clustering customer feedback into themes. Once a team has embeddings, these quick wins become cheap, which is a useful roadmap insight.

They store numbers representing meaning; the text is stored separately.
Any embedding model works for any language.
Quality varies a lot by language and domain.
Embeddings understand exact codes.

A vector database stores vectors with their original text and metadata, and uses approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) indexes to search millions in milliseconds, trading a tiny bit of accuracy for huge speed.

p: Keyword (lexical) search finds documents containing the exact words you typed; BM25 is the standard ranking method. Semantic search finds documents with similar meaning using embeddings. Each fails where the other shines.

Hybrid search runs both and merges the ranked lists (commonly with reciprocal rank fusion). Query 'refund policy for SKU-4471': keyword search nails the product code; semantic search finds 'returns and exchanges' sections that never use the word refund. Together they return both. Many production RAG systems add a reranker afterwards to order the combined results.

Too many results bury the right one.

p: There are three main ways to make a general model work for your use case. Prompting changes the instructions. RAG changes what knowledge the model sees at question time. Fine-tuning changes the model itself by further training it on your examples. They solve different problems, and most teams use the first two long before the third.

This keeps decisions evidence-based.

p: A neural network is layers of simple units connected by weights. Each unit takes numbers in, multiplies them by weights, adds them up, and passes the result on through an activation function. Stack many layers and the network can represent very complex patterns: recognising faces, translating languages, predicting the next word. 'Deep learning' just means many layers.

p: Imagine a sound engineer with a desk of a billion dials, trying to make every song sound right. Training is that, with maths doing the nudging.

p: The same model sits behind all four. What changes is what Claude can see and what it is allowed to do. In a chat it sees only the conversation. In a Project it also sees the files and instructions you added. In Claude Code it can open any file in the repository and, with your permission, run commands and change things.

A Project bundles knowledge (uploaded documents) with instructions (how Claude should behave in every chat inside it). Upload the programme charter, architecture notes and last quarter's decisions, add an instruction such as 'Answer as our TPM; flag risks first', and every new chat starts informed.

When the knowledge gets large, Claude retrieves the relevant parts rather than reading everything each time (the RAG idea from the AI Fundamentals lesson). Good file names and clean documents improve what it finds.

When the output is something you'll come back to, ask for it as an artifact: a status page, a decision log, a calculator, a clickable mock-up. Artifacts can be revised in place and shared by link. The first version of this learning hub was an artifact, built entirely by describing what was needed.

p: Projects reuse libraries other people wrote. A package manager (npm for JavaScript, pip for Python) downloads them from a registry and installs them. The project declares what it accepts (for example 'version 2.x'), and the lock file records exactly what was installed, so every machine and every build gets the same versions.
Without a lock file, two installs a week apart can pull different versions, which is a classic cause of 'it worked yesterday'. Commit the lock file.

Settings that differ between machines or must stay secret (database address, JWT secret, API keys) are read from environment variables instead of being written in code. Locally they live in .env; in production they're set in the hosting platform's settings.
The rule: .env is ignored by Git and never shared; .env.example is committed so a new person knows which variables to set.

p: A five-minute repo health check: is there a README that explains how to run it, a lock file, a .env.example, a sensible .gitignore, and CI that runs tests? Missing pieces predict onboarding pain and fragile releases.
When a vendor or contractor hands over code, check these files first. Secrets committed in history or no lock file are red flags worth raising before acceptance.

Postman acts as the client, just like the browser or the mobile app would. That lets you test the back end on its own and see exactly what it returns.

Before filing a bug, reproduce it in Postman. If the API returns the wrong data, it's a back-end bug; if the API is right but the screen is wrong, it's front end. That one step routes the ticket correctly and saves a day of back-and-forth.
Keep a smoke-test collection for each product you manage: log in, fetch the main data, perform the key action. Running it after a release takes two minutes and catches the obvious breaks.

p: When a site uses Cloudflare, users connect to Cloudflare's nearest data centre first. Cloudflare answers what it can (cached files, blocked attacks) and forwards the rest to your own servers, called the origin.

p: A Worker is a small function that runs on Cloudflare's network for each request, without you managing a server. Typical uses: redirect rules, adding headers, a small API, A/B routing, or calling an AI model and returning the result. They start fast and you pay for usage, which makes them a cheap home for small tools.
Cloudflare also offers storage and AI products around Workers. For a TPM the important point is architectural: some logic can live at the edge, which changes where bugs, logs and costs appear.

Because so much of the internet runs through a few providers, an outage at one can take down many unrelated sites at once. In incident reviews, ask which parts of the user journey depend on each provider, and what the fallback is.
During incidents, check provider status pages (Cloudflare, your cloud, your CDN) early. Many 'our site is down' events are upstream, and knowing quickly changes the communication plan.
In architecture reviews, ask which requests go through the CDN, what is cached and for how long. Stale caches cause confusing bugs: users see old content after a release.

It speeds up cacheable content; slow APIs and databases stay slow.
Cloudflare is only for big companies.
Its free and low-cost tiers are widely used by small sites and side projects.
Edge code replaces the back end.
It's suited to small, fast tasks; core logic and data usually stay at the origin.

Will a CDN speed up a slow database query?

Name two uses for Cloudflare Workers.
Redirects, header changes, small APIs, A/B routing, calling AI models.
Why does a Cloudflare outage break many sites at once?
Many sites route their traffic through Cloudflare's network.

p: Code review means someone other than the author examines a change before it merges. The goal is to keep the codebase healthy over time, not to make each change perfect. Google's published guidance says to approve a change once it clearly improves the overall health of the code, even if it isn't perfect.

p: Ward Cunningham's metaphor: taking a shortcut is like borrowing money. You get speed now (the principal), and then every future change in that area costs extra effort (the interest) until you pay it back by cleaning up.

Martin Fowler adds a useful split: debt can be deliberate or inadvertent, and prudent or reckless. 'We must ship now and will fix it next sprint' is deliberate and prudent. 'What's layering?' is inadvertent and reckless.

p: Add review turnaround to your delivery metrics alongside cycle time. If PRs wait two days for review, adding more AI-generated code makes the queue worse, not better.
When engineering asks for debt work, ask for the interest: which features are slowed, by how much, and what breaks more often. Then you can trade it against roadmap items honestly.

p: An API key is a password for software. Anyone who has it can spend your money and read whatever your account can reach. Keep it in an environment variable (the SDKs read ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY or OPENAI_API_KEY automatically), in a .env file locally and in the hosting platform's secret settings in production. An SDK builds the request for you and adds retries, types and streaming helpers. The underlying call is identical, so anything you learn with raw requests in Postman applies when engineers use the SDK.

p: You send the whole conversation every time: a list of turns alternating between user and assistant, plus an optional system prompt with standing instructions. The API is stateless; it doesn't remember previous calls, so your application stores the conversation and sends it again. That is why long conversations cost more: every turn resends everything before it.

sections.flowLabel: Tool use loop: app sends tools, Claude asks for a tool, app runs it and returns the result, Claude answers
p: You describe each tool with a name, a description and a JSON schema for its inputs. When Claude decides a tool would help, it replies with a tool_use block instead of a final answer. Your code runs the function and sends the result back in a tool_result block; Claude then answers using it.

Client tools run in your code, so you control exactly what happens. Server tools, such as web search, are run by Anthropic and return results in the same response. Either way, your code decides what a tool is allowed to do, which is where safety lives.

sections.h: Prompt caching: pay once for the repeated part
p: Many products send the same large prefix with every request: tool definitions, a long system prompt, a policy document. Prompt caching lets the API reuse the processed prefix. You mark the end of the reusable part with cache_control, keeping the stable content at the start (tools, then system, then messages).

Reading from the cache is billed at a small fraction of the normal input price, and writing to it costs a little more than normal. Entries expire after a few minutes by default, with a longer, more expensive option. Cached reads also don't count towards input-token rate limits on most models, which raises your effective capacity.

p: Structured outputs is the evolution of JSON mode: both produce valid JSON, but only structured outputs guarantees it matches your schema. Engineers usually define the schema in code with Pydantic (Python) or Zod (JavaScript), and the SDK converts it.

Remember that the format is guaranteed, not the facts. A schema-perfect answer can still contain a wrong date or an invented owner. You still need validation, evaluation and, for important actions, human review.

By default the API returns the complete reply in one response, which for a long answer means the user stares at a spinner. With streaming (stream set to true), the server sends the reply in small events as tokens are generated, using server-sent events. The Responses API sends typed events, such as text deltas and a final completed event, so the front end can render text as it arrives.

Streaming improves perceived speed, not total time. It also complicates things: an error can arrive halfway through a reply, and structured output arrives as partial JSON that only becomes valid at the end.

p: Gemini models accept text, images, documents, audio and video in the same request, and can answer questions about them, caption them, classify them or extract data. You can pass small images inline as base64 data, reference a public URL, or upload larger or reused files with the Files API and refer to them.

Model families come in tiers: fast, cheap models for volume and more capable models for hard reasoning. New versions arrive every few months, previews come and go, and older versions are retired. The Gemini 1.5 and 2.0 models listed in older study material are no longer current.

Treat the model ID as a dependency with an end-of-life date. Keep it in configuration rather than scattered through code, track provider deprecation notices, and re-run your evaluation set whenever you change models.

Gemini can be constrained to return JSON matching a schema, or one value from a fixed list (an enum), which is ideal for classification. Asking for JSON in the prompt alone doesn't guarantee JSON; passing a schema does. The Google GenAI SDKs accept schemas defined with Pydantic or Zod, like OpenAI's.

p: A model's parameters (or weights) are the numbers adjusted during training. '8B' means about 8 billion of them. A checkpoint is a saved snapshot of those numbers at a point in training or release; model versions are checkpoints given names.

Rule of thumb: memory for the weights is parameters x bytes per parameter. Running the model needs extra memory on top, mainly for the KV cache that grows with context length. That's why a 7B model quantized to 4 bits downloads as roughly 4 GB.

Quantization stores weights at lower precision to save memory and often speed up inference, while trying to keep accuracy. Going from 16-bit to 8-bit usually costs little quality; 4-bit is a popular sweet spot for local use; very low bit-widths degrade more noticeably. Some methods calibrate on sample data to lose less quality.
The practical rule: a larger model at 4-bit often beats a smaller model at full precision for the same memory, but always test on your task.

p: As a model reads context, it computes intermediate values (keys and values) for every token. The KV cache stores them so they aren't recomputed for each new token. It makes generation much faster, but it takes memory that grows with context length and with the number of simultaneous users, which is why long-context serving is often limited by memory rather than raw computing power.
Batching runs many users' requests through the GPU together. Continuous batching adds and removes requests as they start and finish, instead of waiting for a whole batch.

vLLM is an open-source serving engine from UC Berkeley. Its key idea, PagedAttention, manages the KV cache like an operating system manages memory: in fixed-size blocks that don't need to sit next to each other. That wastes far less memory, so more requests fit on the same GPU. In the authors' published benchmarks this gave many times higher throughput than earlier serving approaches. Other serving stacks use similar ideas.
Write performance requirements in these terms: time to first token, tokens per second, concurrent users and context length at peak. Vague 'should be fast' requirements lead to expensive surprises.
Long context windows are a cost driver when self-hosting. Ask whether the product truly needs them or whether retrieval can keep prompts short.
